title: Storage & Data Stores
summary: Where bytes live, and which store to name. 8 building blocks drilled by recall: the signal that says reach for one, what it costs, how it breaks, which sibling rules it out, and what it is doing across the canonical problems.
keyTakeaways: Relational Database — Row storage with a fixed schema, joins, secondary indexes and multi-row ACID transactions.
Key-Value Store — A hash table with an operations team: get and put by key, partitioned across nodes, no query language.
Document Store — Key-value where the value is a structured document the engine can index and query inside.
Wide-Column Store — Partition-key-first storage (Cassandra, HBase, DynamoDB) built for enormous write volume and range scans within a partition.
Time-Series Store — A store specialised for append-only timestamped measurements, with automatic downsampling, retention and time-range queries.
Object / Blob Storage — Cheap, effectively unbounded storage for immutable files addressed by key, with HTTP access and lifecycle tiering.
Chunking — Splitting a large payload into independently addressable pieces, so transfer, retry, dedup and parallelism operate per piece.

questions.prompt: A design prompt says: The prompt says money, inventory, bookings, or anything where a partial write is a bug with a lawyer attached; Entities are related and access patterns are not known up front — joins buy you flexibility. Which building block answers that, and why is it the right reach?
points: Relational Database — Row storage with a fixed schema, joins, secondary indexes and multi-row ACID transactions.
The prompt says money, inventory, bookings, or anything where a partial write is a bug with a lawyer attached
Entities are related and access patterns are not known up front — joins buy you flexibility
You need read-your-writes and cross-row invariants enforced by the store
questions.answer: Relational Database. Row storage with a fixed schema, joins, secondary indexes and multi-row ACID transactions. You reach for it when: The prompt says money, inventory, bookings, or anything where a partial write is a bug with a lawyer attached; Entities are related and access patterns are not known up front — joins buy you flexibility; You need read-your-writes and cross-row invariants enforced by the store.

questions.prompt: You put Relational Database in a design. Name the signals that should have stopped you — and what it costs even when it is the right call.
points: Write volume that exceeds one primary and the data has no clean partition key
Schemaless, high-churn documents where every row would be half null
Append-only telemetry at millions of events per second
Vertical scaling has a ceiling and horizontal scaling means sharding you implement yourself
Schema migrations on large tables are an operational event, not a deploy
Joins that were free at 1M rows are a capacity plan at 1B
questions.answer: Don't reach for it when: Write volume that exceeds one primary and the data has no clean partition key; Schemaless, high-churn documents where every row would be half null; Append-only telemetry at millions of events per second. And it is never free: Vertical scaling has a ceiling and horizontal scaling means sharding you implement yourself; Schema migrations on large tables are an operational event, not a deploy; Joins that were free at 1M rows are a capacity plan at 1B.

questions.prompt: Relational Database is in your design and load goes up ten times. How does it break?
points: Lock contention on a hot row serialises the whole workload
Connection exhaustion from an app tier that scaled out faster than the pool
An unindexed query pattern discovered in production as a full table scan
questions.answer: Lock contention on a hot row serialises the whole workload Connection exhaustion from an app tier that scaled out faster than the pool An unindexed query pattern discovered in production as a full table scan

questions.prompt: Relational Database vs Key-Value Store vs Wide-Column Store — what decides between them?
points: Key-Value Store — If every access is by primary key and you need no transactions, a KV store scales further for less.
Wide-Column Store — When write volume and partition-key access dominate and you can give up joins.
Relational Database — Row storage with a fixed schema, joins, secondary indexes and multi-row ACID transactions.
questions.answer: Key-Value Store: If every access is by primary key and you need no transactions, a KV store scales further for less. Wide-Column Store: When write volume and partition-key access dominate and you can give up joins.

questions.prompt: Relational Database appears in 4 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Payment System (Wallet / Ledger) — Holds the ledger, where a partial write is not a degraded mode but a lost or duplicated payment — the case ACID exists for.
Design a Ticket Booking System (Ticketmaster-style) — Enforces seat uniqueness transactionally; overselling is the specific failure this store is chosen to make impossible.
Design a Prescription Drug Marketplace — Holds orders, authorisations and the dispensing audit trail, where regulatory correctness outranks throughput.
Design an Authentication & Session Service — The user and credential store — modest volume, strong consistency, and the place a password change must take effect immediately.
questions.answer: Relational Database carries different work in each: in Design a Payment System (Wallet / Ledger), holds the ledger, where a partial write is not a degraded mode but a lost or duplicated payment — the case ACID exists for. in Design a Ticket Booking System (Ticketmaster-style), enforces seat uniqueness transactionally; overselling is the specific failure this store is chosen to make impossible. in Design a Prescription Drug Marketplace, holds orders, authorisations and the dispensing audit trail, where regulatory correctness outranks throughput. in Design an Authentication & Session Service, the user and credential store — modest volume, strong consistency, and the place a password change must take effect immediately.

You need very high throughput and predictable single-digit-millisecond latency

You reach for it when: Every access in the prompt is 'look this up by its id'; You need very high throughput and predictable single-digit-millisecond latency; The value is opaque to the store — a session, a blob of JSON, a serialized object.

points: You will need to query by anything other than the key; you would be building indexes by hand
Cross-key transactions or invariants

points: Hot partition from a key design that concentrates traffic
Unbounded value growth turning one key into a multi-megabyte read
Eventual consistency surfacing as a read that does not contain the write you just made
questions.answer: Hot partition from a key design that concentrates traffic Unbounded value growth turning one key into a multi-megabyte read Eventual consistency surfacing as a read that does not contain the write you just made

questions.prompt: Key-Value Store vs Relational Database vs Document Store — what decides between them?
points: Relational Database — The moment two rows must change together, you want transactions more than you want throughput.
Document Store — Same key-based access but with queryable structure inside the value.
Key-Value Store — A hash table with an operations team: get and put by key, partitioned across nodes, no query language.
questions.answer: Relational Database: The moment two rows must change together, you want transactions more than you want throughput. Document Store: Same key-based access but with queryable structure inside the value.

questions.prompt: Key-Value Store appears in 7 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a URL Shortener — Holds the short-code → URL mapping. Every access is a lookup by key, which is the shape a KV store scales furthest on.
Design a Distributed Rate Limiter — Holds per-client counters keyed by client and window, where the entire access pattern is read-modify-write on a single key.
Design a Leaderboard — Sorted sets are the leaderboard — score updates and top-N range reads are both native operations rather than queries.
Design a Distributed Job Scheduler — Stores per-job execution state keyed by job id, written and read far more often than it is queried.
Design a Proximity Service — Holds current entity locations keyed by id, overwritten on every ping rather than appended to.
Design a Feature Store — The online store itself: features keyed by entity id, read at single-digit-millisecond latency on the inference path.
Design an Authentication & Session Service — Holds sessions and refresh tokens keyed by id, with TTL doing the expiry work the application would otherwise schedule itself.
questions.answer: Key-Value Store carries different work in each: in Design a URL Shortener, holds the short-code → URL mapping. Every access is a lookup by key, which is the shape a KV store scales furthest on. in Design a Distributed Rate Limiter, holds per-client counters keyed by client and window, where the entire access pattern is read-modify-write on a single key. in Design a Leaderboard, sorted sets are the leaderboard — score updates and top-N range reads are both native operations rather than queries. in Design a Distributed Job Scheduler, stores per-job execution state keyed by job id, written and read far more often than it is queried. in Design a Proximity Service, holds current entity locations keyed by id, overwritten on every ping rather than appended to. in Design a Feature Store, the online store itself: features keyed by entity id, read at single-digit-millisecond latency on the inference path. in Design an Authentication & Session Service, holds sessions and refresh tokens keyed by id, with TTL doing the expiry work the application would otherwise schedule itself.

questions.prompt: You put Document Store in a design. Name the signals that should have stopped you — and what it costs even when it is the right call.
points: Data is highly relational and the same fact would be duplicated across many documents
You need multi-document transactions as the normal case, not the exception

points: Documents grow past the engine's size limit and writes start failing

questions.prompt: Document Store vs Relational Database vs Inverted Index / Search — what decides between them?
points: Relational Database — When the same entity is read in many different shapes, normalise and join instead of duplicating.
Inverted Index / Search — For full-text or faceted query over documents, a search engine is the right tool.
Document Store — Key-value where the value is a structured document the engine can index and query inside.
questions.answer: Relational Database: When the same entity is read in many different shapes, normalise and join instead of duplicating. Inverted Index / Search: For full-text or faceted query over documents, a search engine is the right tool.

questions.prompt: Document Store appears in 3 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Photo-Sharing Service — Holds photo metadata — a self-contained record read as a whole, with fields that vary by capture source.

points: Query patterns are unknown or will change — the partition key is close to irreversible
You need joins, or transactions spanning partitions
The dataset is small enough that one relational primary would do

Tombstones and compaction are operational concerns that leak into latency
Eventual consistency by default; strong reads cost latency and availability

points: Unbounded partition growth turning one partition into a hotspot and then a timeout
Tombstone accumulation making range scans progressively slower until compaction catches up

questions.prompt: Wide-Column Store vs Time-Series Store vs Key-Value Store — what decides between them?
points: Time-Series Store — If every row is a timestamped measurement, a purpose-built TSDB gives you retention and rollups for free.
Key-Value Store — When you never need range scans within a partition, plain KV is simpler.
Wide-Column Store — Partition-key-first storage (Cassandra, HBase, DynamoDB) built for enormous write volume and range scans within a partition.
questions.answer: Time-Series Store: If every row is a timestamped measurement, a purpose-built TSDB gives you retention and rollups for free. Key-Value Store: When you never need range scans within a partition, plain KV is simpler.

questions.prompt: Wide-Column Store appears in 3 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.

Design an Observability Platform — Holds telemetry partitioned by series, chosen because ingest volume is the defining constraint and queries never span partitions.
questions.answer: Wide-Column Store carries different work in each: in Design a Chat System, messages partitioned by conversation and clustered by time, so 'the last 50 in this thread' is one contiguous read. in Design an Ad Click Aggregator, absorbs the raw click firehose, where write throughput is the constraint and reads are always a range within one key. in Design an Observability Platform, holds telemetry partitioned by series, chosen because ingest volume is the defining constraint and queries never span partitions.

questions.prompt: A design prompt says: The prompt is metrics, telemetry, IoT readings, or click events keyed by time; Old data becomes less valuable at a predictable rate and can be rolled up. Which building block answers that, and why is it the right reach?

High-cardinality dimensions per point; label cardinality is the classic way to melt one
You need transactional guarantees or joins

Another store class to operate and to back up

points: Cardinality explosion from a label like user_id or request_id
Queries spanning long windows at full resolution overwhelming memory
Late-arriving points landing after a window was already rolled up

questions.prompt: Time-Series Store vs Stream Processing vs Wide-Column Store — what decides between them?
points: Stream Processing — If the aggregate matters more than the raw points, compute it in-flight and never store them.
Wide-Column Store — A generic partition-by-entity, cluster-by-time table when you need control over the layout.
Time-Series Store — A store specialised for append-only timestamped measurements, with automatic downsampling, retention and time-range queries.
questions.answer: Stream Processing: If the aggregate matters more than the raw points, compute it in-flight and never store them. Wide-Column Store: A generic partition-by-entity, cluster-by-time table when you need control over the layout.

Access needs to be transactional with your database
Latency requirements are single-digit milliseconds
Eventually-consistent listing and metadata in many implementations

Two systems now hold related state — the object and the row that describes it

Hot prefixes throttling throughput in stores that partition by key prefix

questions.prompt: Object / Blob Storage vs Chunking vs CDN — what decides between them?
points: Chunking — For very large or resumable payloads, chunk before you store — it changes the failure story entirely.

questions.answer: Chunking: For very large or resumable payloads, chunk before you store — it changes the failure story entirely. CDN: Blob storage holds the bytes; a CDN is how users actually get them without paying origin egress.

questions.prompt: Object / Blob Storage appears in 5 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Photo-Sharing Service — Holds the original photos and their derived sizes; the database stores only metadata and the object key that points at them.
Design a Video Streaming Service — Stores raw uploads and every transcoded rendition, which is why storage cost multiplies by the size of the bitrate ladder.
Design a File Sync / Object Storage Service — The backing store for content-addressed chunks, with the file manifest in a database pointing at each one.
Design a RAG / Semantic Search System — Holds the source documents the citations point back at, because a retrieved passage without its original is not verifiable.

Design a Business Verification Pipeline — The uploaded document is evidence with the same retention obligation as the decision, so the original is content-addressed and never replaced by anything derived from it.

questions.prompt: Chunking vs Object / Blob Storage vs Deduplication — what decides between them?

questions.prompt: A design prompt says: The prompt implies heavy duplication — shared files, re-uploads, mirrored pages; Storage or bandwidth cost is an explicit constraint. Which building block answers that, and why is it the right reach?

Hashing on the write path, and a content-address index that must itself scale
